<p class="eyebrow">Research questions, contributions, and methods</p>
<p class="lede">My research concerns credit-risk model updating under distribution shift and diagnostic methods for extreme losses. I examine how limited data affect model selection, predictive accuracy, and the reliability of tail-risk estimates.</p>

<p class="meta">The three studies below are manuscripts in preparation, not published or accepted papers. <a href="https://orcid.org/0009-0002-5110-8102">ORCID profile</a> · <a href="https://github.com/sdbambil1">GitHub</a></p>

## Tail Model Diagnostics Using Expected Shortfall and Bounded Loss Layers with an Application to Fire Losses {#fire-loss}

<p class="authors">Silas Bambil, Shudeshna Nandy, Clement Ampong, Prakash Karki, and Chi-Kuang Yeh</p>

**Research question.** Can fitted tail models agree on high-loss quantiles while giving materially different estimates of expected tail losses?

::: {.finding}
**Contribution.** Using established stop-loss identities, the study develops bounded-layer diagnostics and inferential procedures to assess where empirical loss distributions and fitted tail models disagree.

**Principal finding.** Agreement in aggregate tail summaries need not imply agreement within relevant loss layers. Simulations distinguish discrepancy detection from localization and show why identifying a difference does not establish where it occurs.
:::

<details class="methods"><summary>Study design and application</summary>

The study uses Peaks-Over-Threshold and Generalized Pareto modeling, bounded-layer expectations, simulation, and uncertainty assessment. Its empirical application considers structure-fire losses recorded in the 2016–2025 U.S. National Fire Incident Reporting System releases. Particular attention is given to sparse extreme observations and the influence of exceptionally large incidents.

</details>

## Selection Regret in Credit-Risk Model Updating Under Distribution Shift: The Role of Recent Labeled Information {#selection-regret}

<p class="authors">Silas Bambil</p>

**Research question.** Does more frequent selection of the best fitted updating policy necessarily reduce the predictive cost of choosing another policy?

::: {.finding}
**Contribution.** The study distinguishes how often an updating policy is selected correctly from the predictive regret of choosing a different fitted candidate, and evaluates how both measures change with the amount of recent labeled data.

**Principal finding.** In simulations, a larger recent labeled sample reduced mean selection regret without consistently improving agreement with the best fitted candidate. Selection frequency alone is therefore insufficient to characterize decision quality.
:::

<details class="methods"><summary>Study design and evidence</summary>

Simulation experiments compare model-updating choices under different shift conditions and adaptation-sample sizes. Stratified cross-validation is used for policy selection, and independent evaluation data are used to measure predictive loss. A historical mortgage-data application provides an additional comparison. Results are interpreted in terms of fitted-candidate regret rather than an unattainable population oracle.

</details>

<div class="tags"><span>Credit risk</span><span>Selection regret</span><span>Validation</span><span>Distribution shift</span></div>
:::

::: {.paper}

## Selecting and Estimating Credit-Risk Model Updates Under Distribution Shift {#distribution-shift}

<p class="authors">Silas Bambil and Shudeshna Nandy</p>

**Research question.** How should limited labeled data be allocated between selecting a credit-risk model update and estimating the updated model?

::: {.finding}
**Contribution.** The study compares validation-guided selection with unrestricted and regularized refitting under a common labeled-data budget, separating the costs of intervention selection and parameter estimation.

**Principal finding.** Validation-guided selection can improve on unrestricted full-budget refitting when adaptation data are scarce, but does not uniformly outperform regularized full-budget estimation. The best use of labeled data depends on the shift and the available sample.
:::

<details class="methods"><summary>Study design and methods</summary>

The study uses historical mortgage cohorts and controlled simulations under covariate, baseline-risk, and predictor-effect shifts. It compares retention, recalibration, unrestricted and regularized refitting, validation allocation, and post-selection refitting, with independent assessment of predictive performance.

</details>

<div class="tags"><span>Calibration</span><span>Predictive stability</span><span>Logistic regression</span><span>Model updating</span></div>
